Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette:
Tama Faleolo is a 63-year-old Samoan-American man who has been a commercial airline pilot for nearly three decades, a career he built in the years following his service in the Pacific theatre during a period of regional conflict. He is married, the father of grown children, and by most outward appearances a man of considerable professional accomplishment. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 75, describing himself in the intake session as someone who no longer recognises the person he has become.

The event that organises Tama's current presentation occurred during a night combat operation when he was in his mid-twenties. His unit had taken fire during a helicopter extraction; the aircraft went down in partial darkness, and Tama spent hours in the wreckage before rescue, in sustained physical contact with the bodies of men he had served alongside. The specific texture of the torn canvas webbing and blood-soaked fabric he gripped throughout that night left an impression that has never fully released him. The low thudding of rotor blades, which he could hear in the distance during the wait, became inseparable in his nervous system from the terror of that vigil. And the time - late evening, around 2100 hours - remains a threshold his body remembers before his mind does.

In the decades that followed, these sensory details did not fade but sharpened. Tama reports that the memory itself has a strange, dissociated quality - it feels, he says, like it belongs to someone else, like watching footage of a stranger - and yet when it surfaces, the terror it carries is entirely his own, immediate and total, as though no time has passed at all. This quality of the memory - both alien and annihilating - has become a source of its own dread, because Tama cannot predict when something in his surroundings will pull the full memory back without warning. The memory, once activated, floods him with a sense of present danger that extends well beyond the recollection itself, leaving him scanning rooms for exits, tracking the movements of people around him, and unable to settle his nervous system for hours. The hypervigilant state that follows a memory intrusion in turn makes him more susceptible to the next one - the heightened arousal lowers his threshold, so that sounds and textures he might otherwise absorb now catch him and drag him back.

His occupation places him in direct daily contact with his most potent trigger. The cockpit of a commercial aircraft is filled with the sounds of engines and, on certain approaches or in certain weather conditions, the unmistakable percussive rhythm of nearby rotor craft. When Tama hears a helicopter during a flight - during a pre-departure hold, a coastal approach, or an air traffic interaction - his body responds before any conscious appraisal occurs. His hands tighten, his chest constricts, and the threshold for the memory collapses. That the trigger arrives within the professional context he has spent his adult life building has deepened his sense that something is fundamentally wrong with him. He has come to believe, with a quiet but entrenched conviction, that a man who cannot hear a helicopter without trembling is defective in some essential way - broken at a level that precedes circumstance. This appraisal of himself as damaged does not remain contained; it bleeds into his reading of the world more broadly, confirming for him that danger is everywhere and that his inability to feel safe is simply an accurate perception of reality rather than a symptom of injury.

The nights are worst. Tama finds that after approximately 2100 hours, a generalised unease settles over him that he cannot reason away, and his wife has noted that he becomes withdrawn and watchful in the evenings in ways that have quietly eroded the intimacy between them. His belief that he is fundamentally miserable now - that the happy man he once was is simply gone - has made it harder for him to reach toward her or accept reassurance, because he has come to understand his unhappiness not as a wound but as a verdict.

What finally brought Tama to seek help was a near-incident during a landing approach - not a mechanical failure, but a moment in which a low-flying helicopter passed close enough that he froze at the controls for several seconds. His co-pilot noticed. Tama is terrified of losing his licence, but more than that, he is afraid of what it would mean to have nothing left to prove he is still the man he once was.
